Jacquelyn Martin - AP Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save The U.S. military says it’s carrying out its 10th consecutive night of strikes on Iran in a push to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. Central Command said on social media that the strikes “are designed to further degrade Iranian military capabilities used to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.” The strikes have escalated as the U.S. and Iran vie for control of the crucial energy shipping route, with Tehran retaliating by launching attacks on American allies Kuwait, Jordan and Bahrain. President Donald Trump earlier warned on social media that “Every time Iran kills an American Soldier they will pay for that killing many times over!” The U.S., early Monday, launched a ninth night of airstrikes on Iran after announcing the death of another American service member killed in Iraq during the “controlled detonation” of a downed Iranian drone. The U.S. military also identified two soldiers who were killed in Jordan on Friday while defending against Iranian ballistic missile and drone attacks. Seventeen U.S. troops have been killed since the start of the war. The Latest: Trump 50% tariff targets Canadian autos, alcohol and cheese The president has imposed 50% tariffs on most Canadian goods, declaring that Canada has unfairly discriminated against American autos, alcohol and dairy products. The move, announced Monday, could unleash a new wave of economic chaos, with risks of higher inflation and further fraying of relations between two nations that had been closely woven together before Trump’s return to the White House. The administration official previewing the action said that Canada was one of the only nations other than China that retaliated against Trump’s previous tariffs and must be held accountable. The official insisted on anonymity on a call with reporters to preview the president’s actions. More US strikes start up against Iran The U.S. military says it’s carrying out its 10th consecutive night of strikes on Iran in a push to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. Central Command said on social media that the strikes “are designed to further degrade Iranian military capabilities used to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.” The strikes have escalated as the U.S. and Iran vie for control of the crucial energy shipping route, with Tehran retaliating by launching attacks on American allies Kuwait, Jordan and Bahrain. Two soldiers were killed in Iranian attacks on a base in Jordan on Friday that left a third service member missing. Separately, another died in Iraq on Saturday during the “controlled detonation” of a downed Iranian drone. President Trump earlier warned on social media that “Every time Iran kills an American Soldier they will pay for that killing many times over!” Trump signs executive order on supply chains for US military Trump on Monday signed an executive order that would expand the Pentagon’s ability to track the raw materials and equipment used in software and gear — with the goal of strengthening domestic supply chains. The order would require government contractors starting in 2027 to prove their need for waivers when domestic materials are not available, Peter Navarro, the president’s senior counselor for trade and manufacturing, said during a call with reporters. The Defense Department would also require contractors to map their critical supply chains from raw materials to the products delivered to the military. Jordan says Iran launched another missile attack Jordan’s armed forces said Monday evening they had shot down three Iranian missiles, adding that there had been no material damage or casualties. There was no immediate word from Iran. Trump will visit Delaware to honor service members killed in Iran war White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Trump will be at Dover Air Force Base on Tuesday evening for the dignified transfer of U.S. service members. “The President and the entire White House are praying for their families,” Leavitt said on social media Monday. Two service members were killed Friday in Jordan while defending against Iranian ballistic missile and drone attacks, the U.S. military said. A third service member was missing after the attack. Another American service member was killed Saturday in northern Iraq in what was described as a controlled detonation of an Iranian ordnance. Trump, in apparent pushback on Mamdani, says Netanyahu won’t be arrested in US The president offered the assurance to Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu after New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani told the New York Times that the Israeli prime minister “belongs in The Hague” and that he was in “active conversation” with the city’s legal department about potentially arresting him if he comes to New York City for the U.N. General Assembly in September. “Benjamin Netanyahu will not be arrested, in any way, shape, or form, while in the United States of America,” Trump said in a social media post in which he made no direct mention of Mamdani. During his mayoral campaign last year, Mamdani said he would order the city’s police to arrest Netanyahu under a warrant issued by the International Criminal Court over Netanyahu’s role in the war in Gaza. Trump threatens harsh response against Iran for targeting of US troops going forward The president took to social media on Monday to warn that “every time Iran kills an American Soldier” going forward “they will pay for that killing many times over.” Trump offered no further details but said his directive has been relayed to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and other U.S. military leaders. Trump’s warning came after the U.S. earlier Monday launched its ninth night of airstrikes on Iran after announcing the death of a U.S. service member, killed in Iraq during the “controlled detonation” of a downed Iranian drone. Seventeen American troops have been killed since the start of the war. British military says a second ship was attacked off the coast of UAE The British military’s United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center said Monday evening that a second ship had been attacked in the Strait of Hormuz, this one off the coast of the United Arab Emirates Earlier, a vessel caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after being hit by a projectile near the coastline of Oman. The crew abandoned the vessel, which was adrift and still ablaze hours later, the UKMTO said. The route around Oman has been the one the U.S. military has encouraged ships to travel to avoid Iran’s control. The Guard later claimed it was targeting tankers in the strait. Tehran also hit U.S.-allied countries throughout the Middle East. Bahrain sounded its missile alert sirens Monday morning, while Kuwait said its air defenses were firing at an incoming Iranian barrage. Bahrain’s Foreign Ministry condemned Iranian drone strikes targeting the country’s air traffic systems, saying they endanger travel for civilians. Ontario’s premier says he’s frustrated with Trump’s wildfire comments Ontario Premier Doug Ford told a news conference Monday he is frustrated with Trump’s threats to place tariffs on Canada over wildfire smoke. Ford said Ontario has contributed to fighting fires in the U.S. and offered assistance when Georgia was struck with a hurricane in 2024. “Rather than criticize and threaten Canada, your closest friend, maybe one day you’re going to need our help,” Ford said. “I get frustrated just listening (to) that bunch of rubbish.” Ford noted one of the largest fires started in Minnesota. “Maybe President Trump would offer his closest allies and friends some support rather than sit there and threaten tariffs.” Nearly 200 wildfires are currently burning across Northern Ontario, with 57 out of control. Trump talked about wildfires with Carney at World Cup Trump said he told Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney he needs to do more to stop wildfires when they talked during Sunday’s FIFA World Cup final in New Jersey. “I told them you got to stop these fires from coming in and poisoning our air. Our air has been poisoned,” Trump told reporters on Sunday when he returned from the game. “If we can help them, we’ll help them. But maybe they should pay us some damages or something, or we should do some tariffs.” Trump last week accused Canada of neglecting forest management. It is unclear under what authority Trump would rely on to impose new tariffs on Canada. Sen. Jon Ossoff fuels reelection campaign by accusing Trump of corruption The Democrat from Georgia is making full-throated broadsides against Trump as he runs for reelection, calling the president a “national disgrace” leading a “Mar-a-Lago mafia” and “the most corrupt administration of all time.” The 39-year-old senator’s approach is being noticed across the Democratic spectrum, from activists hungry for the right message in the 2026 midterms to those pining for viable presidential candidates. And now he has a 20-1 fundraising advantage against Rep. Mike Collins, who won a Republican primary runoff after Trump’s last-minute endorsement. Collins argues that Ossoff is “weak” and “woke,” just another “out-of-touch, far-left liberal.” “The senator is definitely having a moment,” Democratic strategist Lis Smith said, adding that tying Trump’s personal financial gain to his performance on the economy is a strategy “more Democrats should adopt.” Justice Department activates untested ‘alien terrorist’ deportation court The Justice Department has filed a first-ever petition to a secretive and dormant court created 30 years ago to weigh government requests to deport so-called “alien terrorists” from the United States. The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was established in 1996 but had never received a petition until the Justice Department filed an application last week seeking the removal of an individual whose name is withheld from the single-page document posted on the court’s website. A written response from the chief judge of the five-member court — all appointed by Chief Justice John Roberts — indicates that a hearing was held and that the Justice Department was directed to provide more information on Wednesday. The chief judge of wrote that “the Government could benefit from the opportunity for more thoughtful consideration.” Trump urges review of climate change report used by judges Trump complained that a report on climate change National Academy of Sciences included “discredited” information that created “huge losses” across the country. The report is used by the Federal Judicial Center as a resource to assist judges in considering scientific evidence. Trump ordered “federal suspension and debarment officials” to review the research organization’s conduct, adding that taxpayers should not be funding ″climate fraud” and judges should not rely on the report. It was not clear what officials Trump was referring to and what, exactly, he wants them to investigate. Earlier this year, the judicial center withdrew a chapter on climate change from the newest reference manual on scientific evidence after Republican state attorneys general complained it was biased against fossil fuel companies. The Vances are doing their part to reverse declining birth rates Vice President JD Vance and his wife, second lady Usha Vance , are celebrating the birth of their fourth child. Born Sunday, Alec Neel Vance joins older siblings Ewan, 9; Vivek, 6; and Mirabel, 4. The Vances said Usha and the baby are happy and healthy. They also thanked the doctors and staff at the Walter Reed National Military Medical Center and the White House medical team. The Republican vice president has passionately advocated for Americans to have more children . He repeatedly expressed alarm about declining birth rates as he launched his political career in 2021, and told the 2025 March for Life anti-abortion rally, “I want more babies in the United States of America.” The story behind the Freedom Fuel Trump loves to promote Trump and his White House have enthusiastically promoted the Freedom Fuel Network, a chain of star-spangled convenience stores selling gas at $3.47 per gallon to honor the 47th president. Untangling exactly who is behind the Philadelphia-area venture has proven difficult. Records indicate the chain was launched last month by a collection of businessmen including an NFL kicking coach, a GOP fundraiser and a New Jersey entrepreneur who was ordered along with his brother to pay civil damages for unlawfully taking more than 200,000 gallons of fuel. None of them want to talk about it. How the stations got Trump’s attention remains a mystery. Experts say they’re likely selling the gas for a loss. What is clear: Trump has loved the idea of cheaper gas with average costs per gallon rising above $4 again as the war with Iran continues. ▶ Read more Olympian accused of damaging Reflecting Pool gets a trial date David Hearn, 67, has pleaded not guilty to deliberately damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool amid a troubled multimillion-dollar renovation project championed by Trump. (KOLN) - The Budweiser Clydesdales are back in Lincoln, this time making an appearance at the WarHorse Casino in the southwest part of town. The world-renowned Clydesdales are visiting in support of Anheuser-Busch’s partnership with Folds of Honor, a nonprofit organization that provides families of fallen or disabled U.S. veterans and first responders with academic scholarships. Marc Deleo, WarHorse Gaming’s vice president of marketing, said between WarHorse, Legacy Downs and Quality Brands, which serves Budweiser products at the casino, a total of $10,000 was donated to the nonprofit on Friday. “Everybody’s always excited to see the Clydesdales and get photos,” Deleo said. “We’re real excited to give back to the local community. That’s what we’re all about, Warhorse and Legacy Downs, is giving back to the community here in Lincoln and in Omaha as well, and to Nebraska.” The Clydesdales are currently traveling across the country for community events in partnership with Folds of Honor. Budweiser is also celebrating an anniversary this year, marking 150 years of the brand. If you’d like to support Folds of Honor, those who are 21 and older can purchase Budweiser drinks from now until November at restaurants and bars. A portion of the proceeds totaling up to $1.5 million will be donated to the nonprofit. The Clydesdales will be heading to Wilber on Saturday for the town’s annual Czech Festival. http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/28/tanke.text: A tanker carrying liquefied petroleum gas paid a record $5.3 million (€4.5 million) for priority passage through the Panama Canal ahead of El Niño-related restrictions, the waterway's deputy administrator told AFP on Thursday.South Korean company SK Gas paid the record sum for the G. Spirit to transit the canal on 1 September, two days before authorities are due to reduce the number of daily transits due to the El Niño weather phenomenon, Bloomberg reported.Panama declared an emergency over El Niño on Tuesday as a severe regional drought continues to deplete the water reserves needed to operate the canal.Rainfall deficits have reached up to 60% on the country's Pacific side, while 11 watersheds are already experiencing water stress.Central America is in the throes of a severe drought driven by El Niño, a weather pattern that warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, triggering worldwide changes in winds, atmospheric pressure and rainfall.Ships usually book their Panama Canal passage well in advance, while those without reservations face an average wait of five days. Last-minute slots can also be secured through an auction.The Panama Canal Authority said the average price paid at auction between October 2025 and February 2026 was around $55,000 (€47,000).In April, however, a vessel carrying liquefied natural gas paid $4 million (€3.4 million) to skip the queue and avoid delays as the war in the Middle East increased demand for moving vital cargo through the canal.The waterway, which handles around five percent of global maritime trade, will reduce daily transits from 36 to 34 from 3 September, before cutting them further to 32 later in the month.In 2023 the water level in the lakes feeding the canal was so low the waterway's operators cut the daily ship transit number from 38 to 22.El Niño is expected to intensify in the coming months, with its effects potentially lasting until May 2027.

Photograph: US Marine Corps Forces, South Ecuador US strikes on Ecuadorian fishing boats raise humanitarian concerns but Trump admin not wavering Attorney says fishers ‘losing their livelihoods’, but Marco Rubio maintains US still willing to ‘blow up ships if need be’ Tiago Rogero South America correspondent Sat 26 Sep 2026 12.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 12.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google W hile the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio , was being decorated in Quito by Ecuador’s president for “helping to promote peace in the region”, 10 Ecuadorian fishers whose boat had been blown up by US forces were adrift in the eastern Pacific. View image in fullscreen Ecuador’s president, Daniel Noboa, right, presents the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, with Ecuador’s highest ranking National Order of Merit, the Grand Cross, at Carondelet palace in Quito, on 9 September. Photograph: Dolores Ochoa/AP On 8 September, a day before Rubio arrived, a US patrol vessel intercepted the fishing boat Don Rufo in international waters near Ecuador . “The gringos were all armed as if they were going to war,” said the boat’s captain, Mero Calderón, 50. “I tried to show them our catch to prove that we were there working, but they wouldn’t listen,” he added. View image in fullscreen A US patrol vessel intercepting the fishing boat Don Rufo in international waters near Ecuador. Photograph: US Southern Command/X “They brought two huge bombs aboard, took us to their ship, handcuffed and blindfolded us, and blew our boat to pieces,” said Calderón, who along with five other fishers, was handed over to local authorities. But another 10 crew members were fishing farther out to sea in a smaller boat that was not equipped to make it back to shore. The Ecuadorian navy only rescued them on 10 September, when Rubio was already in Peru preparing to return to the US. View image in fullscreen Ten crew members from the five skiffs belonging to the vessel Don Rufo, after they were located and taken aboard the BAE Atahualpa, following air-maritime search and reconnaissance operations conducted by the Ecuadorian navy. Photograph: Ecuadorian Navy US Southern Command posted an edited 14-second video of the operation and said “intelligence confirmed” that the vessel was being used by a gang as a “floating refuelling station” for speedboats allegedly carrying drugs – which the fishers deny. It was one of eight operations involving Ecuadorian boats in just more than two weeks – the latest on 16 September – to follow the same pattern. Unlike the nearly 70 US airstrikes in the Pacific and Caribbean that have killed 234 people since last year, crews were removed before the vessels were sunk. ‘We were terrified they were going to kill us’: fishers who survived US boat strike speak out Read more View image in fullscreen A still from a video released by US forces intercepting a floating refuelling station supporting illicit at-sea drug trafficking operations in the eastern Pacific. Photograph: US Southern Command @Southcom Also, rather than unilateral US attacks, the new wave of operations has the open support of Ecuador’s far-right president, Daniel Noboa, who is calling them “joint operations”. Donald Trump has compared the drug trafficking operations to the campaign against the Islamic state. “Like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release, which is what we’re doing,” Trump said on Tuesday. Some analysts see the shift as an indication that the US’s military strategy against drug trafficking in Latin America has entered a new phase. View image in fullscreen Marines and sailors with Maritime Raid Force, LCF-24, boarding the Ecuadorian fishing vessel Conquista 2 in the Pacific on 2 September. Photograph: US Marine Corps Forces, South “Noboa has offered Ecuador as a ‘laboratory’ for the implementation of this new phase,” said Will Freeman, a fellow for Latin America studies at the Council on Foreign Relations. Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, over the past decade it has become a major trafficking hub because of its access to the Pacific, including the area where the attacks on boats have been taking place. Noboa has responded with a controversial “iron-fist” approach to the gangs, issuing repeated states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces. View image in fullscreen Relatives of the four minors apprehended by soldiers and found dead near a military base dance during a rally to demand justice a year after their apprehension in Guayaquil, Ecuador on 8 December 2025. Photograph: Marcos Pin/AFP/Getty Images This crackdown however has done little to reduce violence, and instead has eroded human rights . The most notable example of human rights abuse came last year in the case of the “ Guayaquil Four ”, the forced disappearance of four Afro-Ecuadorian boys between the age of 11 and 15. All four boys were found dead, there bodies charred and dismembered. Despite pushback from voters, Noboa signed an agreement with the White House authorising joint operations and granting US military personnel involved in counter-narcotics operations immunity from criminal prosecution. The operations have also extended to land, with US troops taking part in raids last Thursday. “Noboa is interested in the optics of a very lethal crackdown and in making Ecuador a place where the Trump administration can refine those methods and show them off,” said Freeman, who has also reported on the boat attacks in Ecuador for the New Yorker magazine. View image in fullscreen People look at the remains of a burned-out fishing boat in the port of Manta, Ecuador, on 6 June 2026. The Ecuadorian national police said at least 20 fishing boats had been damaged. Photograph: Ariel Ochoa/EPA View image in fullscreen The Ecuadorean army shows drug trafficker Adolfo Macías, alias Fito, being guarded after his recapture in Manta, which is in the Manabi province. Photograph: Ecuadorean Army/AFP/Getty Images Trump has pressured Latin American presidents to join an anti-drug cartel coalition he created called Shield of the Americas . With Peru and Colombia recently joining, the group now includes all but the few countries still governed by the left, such as Mexico and Brazil – where a far-right senator is a serious contender in October’s election. So far, the coalition’s primary goal appears to have been increasing joint operations against alleged drug traffickers. Adam Isacson, director for defence oversight at the Washington Office on Latin America, expects joint operations to expand across the region. View image in fullscreen Fishermen work along the shore as local fishermen are increasingly being pursued by Ecuadorean gangs to move drugs and for their skills navigating the Pacific waters along Ecuador’s coast, in Manta, on 4 June. Photograph: Karen Toro/Reuters Isacson stressed that though more people are being turned over to local authorities instead of killed, the US is “still doing the bad old stuff”. On 19 September, four people were killed in the Caribbean. As with the other airstrikes, the US has not disclosed their identities or any of the alleged evidence linking them to criminal activity. During his trip to Ecuador, Rubio said the decision on what approach to take was “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination” that depended on the threat and location of the boat, but that the US would “still blow up ships if need be”. Human rights organisations have described the airstrikes as extrajudicial killings, and a special rapporteur for the UN human rights council has concluded that there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that they constitute “ crimes against humanity ”. Despite Trump’s claims, available data show they have had no impact on the volume of cocaine entering the country. Journalists and human rights groups have managed to identify some of the victims , who in many cases were innocent or, when suspected of involvement in criminal activity, poor people at the bottom of trafficking networks. View image in fullscreen Relatives wait for 32 crew members to be released under precautionary measures in Manta, Ecuador, on 8 September 2026. The 24 crew members of the Maria Candelaria and eight from the Conquista II face judicial proceedings on suspicion of illicit association and fuel trafficking after their vessels were intercepted and destroyed by US forces in the Pacific Ocean. Photograph: Ariel Ochoa/EPA In Ecuador, the local NGO Permanent Committee for the Defence of Human Rights estimates that more than 220 fishers have been subjected to “violent boardings, arbitrary detentions, enforced disappearances, torture and the destruction of vessels” in this year’s US operations. None of the fishers remains in custody and, while some are still facing prosecution, many have already been acquitted for lack of evidence . “Fishers are losing their livelihoods when the US destroys the boats. Besides, if the US says the vessels were being used to refuel drug boats, why destroy the evidence?” said the committee’s lawyer, Fernando Bastías. A US Southern Command spokesperson said it conducts operations “in compliance with US and international law” and that leaving boats “intact could permit their reuse by criminal networks”. Although the US and Ecuador have celebrated the recent operations on social media, three cases from earlier this year remain unclaimed . The first was on 20 January, when the fishing vessel Fiorella disappeared with eight crew members on board; days earlier, some of them had told relatives they were being monitored by drones and by a vessel on which they said they had seen a US flag. Human rights organisations and journalists identified two more cases with similar patterns in late March, although the fishers survived. The Washington Post reported that the three cases were part of a covert CIA programme, and the agency declined to comment. A US Southern Command spokesperson said it had no knowledge of, nor were its forces “involved in the incidents described in reports involving the Fiorella”. View image in fullscreen Maria Mero and her mother, Maria Cueva, speak during an interview after Mero’s husband Gabriel Aladino Mero Delgado and brother Jefferson Ariel Mero Cueva disappeared from the boat Fiorella after a strike in June 2026. Photograph: Karen Toro/Reuters View image in fullscreen Maria Cueva holding a picture of her son Jefferson Ariel Mero Cueva. Photograph: Karen Toro/Reuters Both the husband and brother of María Mero, 43, were aboard the Fiorella: Gabriel Aladino Mero Delgado, 44, and Jefferson Ariel Mero Cueva, 25. “Where did they take them? Do they have them in the US, in a prison somewhere? We don’t want any trouble; we just want them to send them back to us,” she told the Guardian. The families say they have spent months trying to get answers from the Ecuadorian government, so far without success. “They were fishers, not criminals. Let the great president come here to my house and see whether I have luxuries, anything that would show I’m a drug trafficker. No, because all of us here are poor, and we just want our loved ones back,” added Mero.
